title: Rawls and Nozick: Justice in Modern Society
subtitle: Two Harvard colleagues, one question: who deserves what?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain Rawls' original position and veil of ignorance and why he thought it leads to fair principles.
By the end you will be able to state Rawls' two principles of justice, including the difference principle.
By the end you will be able to explain Nozick's entitlement theory and his Wilt Chamberlain argument against patterned justice.
By the end you will be able to use the experience machine to test whether pleasure is all that matters.
By the end you will be able to weigh the strongest objections to both thinkers.
hook:
Imagine you are about to be born, but you don't yet know into which life. You might arrive as the child of a billionaire or of a refugee, healthy or chronically ill, gifted at mathematics or struggling to read, in a country at peace or at war. Before the dice are rolled, someone hands you a pen and asks you to write the rules of the society you will be born into. What rules would you write?

That thought experiment, published in 1971, revived political philosophy almost overnight. Three years later a colleague down the corridor at Harvard answered with a book that asked a very different question: never mind what rules you would choose behind a curtain; what about the things people have already made, earned and freely exchanged? Who are you to redistribute them? Today we meet John Rawls and Robert Nozick, and the argument between them still shapes every debate about taxes, welfare and inequality.

sections.heading: The Revival of Political Philosophy
sections.body:
By the middle of the twentieth century, many English-speaking philosophers thought the grand questions of politics were finished business. Remember logical positivism on Day 71? If moral statements were just expressions of feeling, then a theory of justice looked like a dressed-up opinion. Philosophers analyzed the meaning of words; they rarely told anyone how to organize a society.

**John Rawls** (1921–2002) changed that. Born in Baltimore, he served as an infantryman in the Pacific during the Second World War, an experience that, by his own later account, shook his religious faith. He spent two decades refining a single idea, and in 1971 published *A Theory of Justice*, a long, careful, sometimes dry book that became one of the most discussed works of philosophy in the century. Its opening line is famous:

> Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought.

Rawls was not mainly asking whether individual people act justly. His subject was the **basic structure** of society: the constitution, the economy, property law, the family, the school system. These institutions shape our lives from before we are born. They decide who gets what kind of start. So, Rawls asked, what would make them fair?

His main target was utilitarianism, which you met on Day 61. Bentham and Mill told us to maximize total happiness. Rawls objected that this treats society like one big person, adding up pleasures and pains across individuals as if one person's suffering could be cancelled by another person's gain. Utilitarianism, he wrote, does not take seriously the distinction between persons. If enslaving a small minority made the majority happy enough, the numbers might come out in favor. Rawls wanted a theory in which each person has an inviolability that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.

sections.heading: The Original Position and the Veil of Ignorance
sections.body:
Rawls' method was a modern version of the **social contract**, the tradition of Hobbes (Day 42), Locke (Day 52), Rousseau (Day 53) and Kant. But his contract is hypothetical, and it is designed to be fair from the start.

Picture a group of rational people meeting to choose the principles that will govern their society. Rawls calls this imaginary meeting the **original position**. The crucial twist is that the choosers sit behind a **veil of ignorance**. They know general facts about economics, psychology and human needs, but they do not know their own particular place: their sex, race, class, talents, health, religion, or even their personal idea of what makes life worth living.

Why the veil? Because knowledge of our own situation corrupts our judgment. A wealthy person tends to find low taxes obviously fair; a healthy person underrates the importance of healthcare. The veil strips away the information that would let anyone rig the rules in their own favor. Whatever principles would be chosen under those conditions, Rawls argued, are fair, because the conditions of choice are fair. He called his view **justice as fairness**.

The idea has deep roots. It echoes Kant's demand (Day 56) that we act only on principles we could will for everyone. It also has an everyday cousin: the old rule for sharing a cake between two children, where one cuts and the other chooses. The cutter, not knowing which slice will be theirs, has every reason to cut evenly.

What would people behind the veil choose? Rawls thought they would reason cautiously. Since the stakes are your whole life and you have no way of estimating the odds of landing anywhere in particular, he argued, you would follow a **maximin** rule: choose the arrangement whose worst possible outcome is best. You would want to make sure that, even if you end up at the bottom, your life is still decent.

sections.heading: Two Principles of Justice
sections.body:
From the original position, Rawls argued, two principles would emerge.

1. **The liberty principle:** each person has an equal right to the most extensive scheme of basic liberties compatible with the same liberties for all. These include freedom of thought and conscience, freedom of speech and assembly, the right to vote and hold office, and protection from arbitrary arrest.
2. Social and economic inequalities are allowed only if they satisfy two conditions: (a) they are attached to positions open to all under **fair equality of opportunity**, and (b) they are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society. Part (b) is the famous **difference principle**.

The principles come in an order of priority. Liberty comes first: you cannot trade away someone's freedom of religion to raise national income. Then fair opportunity, then the difference principle.

The difference principle is subtle and often misunderstood. It does not demand equal outcomes. Rawls accepted that paying surgeons or inventors more might motivate work that benefits everyone, including the poorest. Inequality is permitted, but it must earn its keep: it is justified only if the worst-off are better off than they would be under any alternative arrangement. If a tax cut for the rich made the poorest better off through growth, the difference principle would approve; if it merely made the rich richer, it would not.

Why should the talented not simply keep everything their talents earn? Here Rawls made his most provocative claim. Nobody deserves the genes they were born with, the family that read to them at night, or the society that happens to reward their particular skills. These are results of a **natural lottery**, morally arbitrary from the point of view of justice. Rawls even suggested that the willingness to work hard is itself shaped by fortunate family and social circumstances. A just society, then, does not erase these differences, but it arranges things so that the lucky gain from their luck only in ways that also help the unlucky.

sections.heading: Nozick's Reply: Entitlement and History
sections.body:
**Robert Nozick** (1938–2002) was a younger Harvard colleague, brilliant and restless, who had been a left-wing student before becoming convinced by libertarian arguments. In 1974 he published *Anarchy, State, and Utopia*, a witty, combative book that defended a **minimal state**, sometimes called a night-watchman state, limited to protecting people against force, theft and fraud and enforcing contracts. Anything more, he argued, violates people's rights.

Nozick's alternative to Rawls is the **entitlement theory** of justice. It has three parts:

- **Justice in acquisition:** how people may justly come to own unowned things in the first place (here Nozick drew on Locke's labor theory of property from Day 52, with a version of Locke's proviso that acquisition must not worsen others' situation).
- **Justice in transfer:** how holdings may justly pass from one person to another, by gift, trade or voluntary exchange.
- **Justice in rectification:** how to correct past injustices, such as theft or conquest.

If everyone came to hold what they have through just acquisition and just transfer, then the distribution is just, whatever it looks like. Justice, for Nozick, is **historical**: it depends on how a distribution came about. Rawls' principles, by contrast, are what Nozick called **patterned**: they judge a distribution by whether it fits a certain shape, such as equality or benefit to the worst-off. Utilitarianism is an **end-state** theory, judging only the resulting snapshot.

Think of a Monopoly game. If you want to know whether the player with all the hotels deserves them, you don't stare at the board; you ask whether the dice were fair and nobody stole from the bank. For Nozick, the same goes for a society.

sections.heading: Wilt Chamberlain and the Experience Machine
sections.body:
Nozick's most famous argument uses the basketball star **Wilt Chamberlain**, the biggest draw in the sport at the time. Start, he says, with whatever distribution you think is perfectly just; call it D1. Perhaps everyone has equal shares. Now Chamberlain signs a contract: twenty-five cents from every ticket sold for home games goes straight to him. A million fans happily drop their quarters into a special box to watch him play. At the end of the season Chamberlain has $250,000, far more than anyone else. Call this new distribution D2.

Is D2 unjust? Everyone started with just holdings. Every fan chose freely how to spend their quarter. Nobody else's share was touched. If D1 was just and each step was voluntary, Nozick asks, how could D2 be unjust? His conclusion is a slogan: **liberty upsets patterns**. Any patterned principle can be maintained only by continually interfering in people's free choices, forbidding exchanges or taking from some to give to others. That is why Nozick made his most notorious claim: taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor. Taking some of your wages, he argued, is like forcing you to work some hours for someone else's purposes.

The same book contains a thought experiment that has nothing to do with taxation but has become even more famous: the **experience machine**. Suppose neuroscientists could plug you into a machine that would give you any experiences you wanted: writing a great novel, falling in love, winning a championship. You would float in a tank, believing it all real. Would you plug in for life?

Most people say no, and Nozick thought this shows something important. We want to *do* things, not just have the experience of doing them; we want to *be* a certain kind of person; we want contact with reality. If so, pleasure is not the only thing that matters, and hedonistic utilitarianism (Day 61) is wrong. Notice the link to the rights theory: Nozick saw persons as agents living their own lives, not containers of pleasant sensations.

sections.heading: The Strongest Objections
sections.body:
Both theories have attracted powerful criticism.

Against Rawls:

- **Is maximin really rational?** The economist John Harsanyi argued that people behind a veil of ignorance would maximize average expected utility, which leads back toward utilitarianism. Many people are willing to take some risks for a better chance at a good life.
- **The communitarian critique.** Michael Sandel, in *Liberalism and the Limits of Justice* (1982), argued that the person behind the veil is an empty self, stripped of the commitments and communities that make us who we are. Can someone with no particular values really choose anything? (The Political Philosophy track takes this debate further in its lesson on liberalism and its communitarian critics.)
- **The family.** Susan Moller Okin, in *Justice, Gender, and the Family* (1989), pointed out that Rawls treated the family as part of the basic structure but said little about the unequal division of labor inside it, where many injustices to women begin.

Against Nozick:

- **History is not clean.** Almost no actual property holdings trace back through an unbroken chain of just acquisitions and transfers. Conquest, slavery, colonial seizure and fraud run through the history of every nation. Nozick admitted that his principle of rectification might justify substantial redistribution in practice, but he never worked it out.
- **Starting points matter.** Critics noted that Chamberlain's fans are free, but a child born into poverty has not chosen anything. Can free exchange from unequal starting points produce outcomes that are fair?
- **Is taxation really forced labor?** A worker who pays tax can still choose their job, and enjoys roads, courts and security funded by the state that makes their earnings possible.

Nozick himself later wrote, in *The Examined Life* (1989), that the libertarian position he had defended now seemed to him seriously inadequate, though scholars disagree about how far he actually moved. Rawls revised his own views too, in *Political Liberalism* (1993), asking how citizens with deeply different religions and philosophies can still share a fair political framework. Both men died in 2002, and the argument they began is still very much alive.

keyQuote.source: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971), §1

modernConnection.title: Behind the Veil in Today's Policy Debates
modernConnection.body:
Listen to almost any argument about taxes, welfare or inheritance and you will hear echoes of Rawls and Nozick, even when nobody names them.

Take the debate over **universal basic income**, the proposal that every citizen receive a regular, unconditional payment. A Rawlsian might ask: would people behind the veil of ignorance want a guaranteed floor in an economy where automation could make some skills suddenly worthless? Given maximin reasoning, a secure minimum looks attractive. A Nozickian would ask a different question: where does the money come from? If it comes from taxing people's earnings, then some people are being made to work for others without their consent, however good the cause.

Or consider **inheritance taxes**. Rawls' natural lottery argument applies with special force here: nobody earns the family they are born into, so large inheritances look like pure luck passed down the generations. Nozick replies that a gift is a just transfer like any other. If I may spend my money on myself, why may I not give it to my children?

The two theories also illuminate the gig economy. Ride-share drivers and delivery couriers choose their contracts freely, just as Chamberlain's fans did. But a Rawlsian points out that freedom of contract operates within a basic structure that determines bargaining power, safety nets and the options available. Whether the result is fair depends on whether that structure works to the benefit of the least advantaged.

Where does the comparison break down? Real policy debates are rarely pure. Almost no political party is fully Rawlsian or fully Nozickian, and empirical questions, such as whether a particular tax actually helps or harms the poor, cannot be settled by philosophy alone. Rawls himself insisted his principles applied to the basic structure as a whole, not to individual policies one at a time. But the two thinkers give us something valuable: a way to see that disagreements about money are often disagreements about whether justice is a pattern or a history.

vocabulary.definition: Rawls' imaginary situation in which rational people choose principles of justice for their society under fair conditions.
vocabulary.example: In the original position, nobody can argue for rules that favor their own religion, because nobody knows what their religion will be.

vocabulary.definition: The device in the original position that hides from the choosers their own particular traits, social position and conception of the good.
vocabulary.example: Behind the veil of ignorance, you might vote for good public hospitals because you don't know whether you will be healthy or sick.

vocabulary.definition: Rawls' principle that social and economic inequalities are justified only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.
vocabulary.example: Under the difference principle, higher pay for doctors is acceptable if it results in better healthcare for the poorest citizens too.

vocabulary.definition: A decision rule: choose the option whose worst possible outcome is better than the worst outcome of the alternatives.
vocabulary.example: A cautious hiker using maximin picks the route whose worst case is a long walk rather than the shortcut whose worst case is a fall.

vocabulary.definition: Nozick's view that a distribution is just if everyone holds what they have through just acquisition, just transfer, or rectification of past injustice.
vocabulary.example: On the entitlement theory, a fortune built from voluntary sales is just, however large it is.

vocabulary.definition: Nozick's term for a principle of justice that requires distributions to fit a particular shape, such as equality or distribution according to need.
vocabulary.example: 'From each according to ability, to each according to need' is a patterned principle.

vocabulary.definition: A state limited to protecting citizens against force, theft and fraud and enforcing contracts; also called the night-watchman state.
vocabulary.example: A minimal state would fund police and courts but not public schools or pensions.

vocabulary.definition: Nozick's thought experiment about a machine that could give you any experiences you wanted, used to test whether pleasure is all that matters.
vocabulary.example: Her refusal to plug into the experience machine convinced her that she valued real achievements, not just the feeling of achievement.

thinkingExercise.title: Writing the Rules Behind the Veil
thinkingExercise.prompt: Put yourself in the original position and design one part of a society's basic structure. Then test your design against Nozick.
steps: Choose one area: healthcare, education, inheritance, or pay for work. Write down the rule you would choose if you did not know whether you would be rich or poor, healthy or sick, talented or not.
Explain your choice in two or three sentences. Did you reason by maximin, protecting the worst case, or were you willing to gamble? Why?
Now imagine a 'Wilt Chamberlain' scenario inside your system: people freely making exchanges that upset your arrangement. Would you allow it, limit it, or correct it afterwards? Justify your answer.
Finally, note one fact about your actual life (your family, talents, or country of birth) that you did nothing to deserve. Does reflecting on it change any of your answers?

summary: Rawls' A Theory of Justice (1971) revived political philosophy by asking what principles would be chosen in a fair original position, behind a veil of ignorance.
Rawls' two principles give priority to equal basic liberties, then require fair equality of opportunity and allow inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged (the difference principle).
Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) answered with an entitlement theory: justice is historical, depending on just acquisition and transfer, not on fitting a pattern.
The Wilt Chamberlain argument claims that liberty upsets patterns; the experience machine suggests we value more than pleasure.
Rawls faces objections about maximin, the 'empty self' and the family; Nozick faces objections about unjust history, unequal starting points and his view of taxation.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of Rawls' veil of ignorance?
options: To ensure that people choose principles that maximize total happiness
To prevent people from tailoring principles of justice to their own particular advantage
To show that people would choose to have no government at all
To prove that human beings are naturally selfish
quiz.explanation: The veil hides each chooser's own position and traits, so nobody can rig the rules in their favor. Rawls was in fact arguing against simple happiness-maximizing.

quiz.question: According to the difference principle, when is an economic inequality justified?
options: Whenever it results from a free market exchange
Never; justice requires equal incomes
Whenever the majority votes for it
When it works to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged
quiz.explanation: Rawls allows inequality, but only when it improves the position of the worst-off compared with alternatives. Free exchange alone is Nozick's test, not Rawls'.

quiz.question: Which statement best captures Nozick's distinction between historical and patterned principles?
options: Historical principles look at how a distribution came about; patterned principles judge whether it fits a shape such as equality
Historical principles apply to ancient societies; patterned principles apply to modern ones
Historical principles require equality; patterned principles allow any distribution
There is no difference; Nozick used the terms interchangeably
quiz.explanation: For Nozick, justice depends on the history of acquisitions and transfers. Patterned principles, like Rawls', judge distributions by their structure.

quiz.question: What conclusion does Nozick draw from the Wilt Chamberlain example?
options: Professional athletes should be taxed more heavily
The original distribution must have been unjust
Maintaining any pattern requires continual interference with people's free choices
Fans are irrational to pay to watch basketball
quiz.explanation: 'Liberty upsets patterns': if just starting holdings are freely exchanged, the pattern dissolves, and keeping it would require restricting or reversing voluntary transactions.

quiz.question: A friend says: 'I'd never plug into a machine that fakes a perfect life; I want my achievements to be real.' Which philosophical point does this best illustrate?
options: Rawls' maximin rule
The experience machine's challenge to the view that pleasure is all that matters
Nozick's principle of rectification
The communitarian critique of the unencumbered self
quiz.explanation: Refusing the experience machine suggests we value doing things and contact with reality, not just pleasant experiences, which challenges hedonism.

quiz.question: Why did Rawls think natural talents do not by themselves give people a moral claim to larger shares?
options: Because talents are always overrated by employers
Because the state owns everyone's talents
Because talented people are usually lazy
Because nobody deserves the genetic and social lottery that gave them their talents
quiz.explanation: Rawls called the distribution of talents and family background a natural lottery, morally arbitrary from the point of view of justice.

quiz.question: Which critic argued that the chooser behind Rawls' veil is an 'empty' self stripped of the community ties that constitute identity?
options: John Harsanyi
Susan Moller Okin
Michael Sandel
Wilt Chamberlain
quiz.explanation: Sandel's communitarian critique targeted Rawls' picture of the self. Harsanyi challenged maximin; Okin focused on justice within the family.

quiz.question: Rawls' liberty principle has priority over the difference principle, so basic liberties may not be sacrificed for economic gains.
quiz.explanation: Rawls ranked the principles: equal basic liberties come first and cannot be traded for greater wealth.

quiz.question: Nozick argued for a state that provides extensive welfare programs funded by progressive taxation.
quiz.explanation: Nozick defended a minimal state limited to protection against force, theft and fraud, and compared taxation of earnings to forced labor.

quiz.question: Rawls' main target in A Theory of Justice was utilitarianism, which he said fails to take seriously the distinction between persons.
quiz.explanation: Rawls objected that summing happiness across people could justify sacrificing some individuals for the greater total.

goDeeper.body:
One of the most interesting developments after Rawls came from his own left. The Marxist philosopher G. A. Cohen argued in *Rescuing Justice and Equality* (2008) that Rawls was too lenient about incentives. If talented people demand higher pay before they will work hard, Cohen asked, isn't that a kind of bargaining that a truly just person would not engage in? In a society whose members really accepted the difference principle, the talented would work productively without demanding extra rewards, and much less inequality would be justified. His slogan, borrowed from the feminist movement, was that the personal is political: justice concerns individual choices, not just institutions.

Meanwhile, a group of philosophers developed **luck egalitarianism** (Ronald Dworkin, Richard Arneson, Cohen again). They distinguished brute luck, which you did not choose (being born blind), from option luck, which results from choices (losing a bet). Justice, they argued, should neutralize brute luck but hold people responsible for their choices. Elizabeth Anderson's influential paper "What Is the Point of Equality?" (1999) attacked this view as harsh and humiliating, since it requires the state to judge whether people's misfortunes were their own fault. She proposed instead **democratic equality**: the point of justice is to let people relate to one another as equals, without domination or oppression.

On the libertarian side, philosophers have tried to fill the gap Nozick left in his theory of rectification, while left-libertarians (such as Hillel Steiner and Michael Otsuka) accept full self-ownership but argue that natural resources belong to everyone equally, which yields surprisingly egalitarian conclusions. The Political Philosophy track explores these debates about legitimacy, liberty and global justice in more depth.

questions: Would you choose maximin behind the veil of ignorance, or would you gamble for a chance at a better life? What does your answer reveal about your attitude to risk and fairness?
If almost all existing property can be traced back to some historical injustice, what would Nozick's principle of rectification actually require today?
Is it fair to say that hard work itself is partly a product of luck, as Rawls suggested? What follows if it is?
